transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 PT   Duration: 47 min
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Leo Martinez (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Horizon - Head of ML), Tom Reed (Horizon - Infra), Priya N. (Horizon - CPO)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, this is Leo our solutions engineer. quick roll call?
[00:07] Aisha: Hi Aisha here.
[00:08] Tom: Tom here.
[00:09] Priya: Priya on my side.
[00:11] Maya: Awesome. The agenda — we want to walk through cost unit economics, understand your workload and constraints, and propose Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private options. we'll leave time for Qs. Sound good?
[00:20] Aisha: Yep. Our core ask is predictable per-query cost for our signals engine. We're doing ~100M tokens/day today in peak, expecting to double in Q3. latency 95th needs to be ~150ms or better for top-tier signals, otherwise trader experience degrades.
[00:35] Maya: Great, can you describe typical sequence lengths and concurrency?
[00:41] Tom: Most queries are short — 12 to 40 tokens median, tails up to 400 tokens when context includes a few docs. concurrency spikes are what worry us, we can see sudden bursts to 600 rps for short queries.
[00:55] Leo: ok, yeah that distribution helps a lot. Two levers we usually call out: batching — combining short requests to improve GPU utilization — and KV/prefix caching for repeated contexts. both can reduce per-token cost substantially but trade off against per-request latency.
[01:10] Aisha: Can you quantify that? like what does batching actually save per-token?
[01:14] Leo: Sure; ballpark numbers: for short-seq workloads, continuous batching can reduce token cost by 20-60% depending on batch depth and model. caching — if you have repeated prefixes or user histories — can reduce tokens generated by 30-80% for those traffic patterns. the math depends on cache hit rate, sequence lengths, and model compute cost.
[01:32] Maya: Also quantization and lower-precision model variants. for many embeddings and non-critical generation tasks, using int8 or 4-bit models reduces GPU time and cost. but for high-sensitivity outputs you may want fp16 or higher-precision.
[01:46] Priya: For us accuracy can't drop more than 2-3% on our signal quality metrics, so quantization needs to be validated.
[01:52] Leo: totally, we can run A/Bs in a pilot. we often recommend running a small eval set to measure quality delta at different quant settings; often 4-bit works for many LLMs, but we validate.
[02:05] Maya: on pricing itself — Hosted is usage-based per-token with transparent unit prices; Dedicated is reserved capacity (monthly commit) with lower per-token equivalents when fully utilized; Private has platform fee plus infra cost and is best when you need VPC/KMS or air-gapped.
[02:24] Aisha: Can you share example math? we want to compare: hosted with volume discounts vs a dedicated 4xA100 pool.
[02:31] Maya: I'll share a spreadsheet after. quick numbers now: imagine a baseline model that costs $0.0025 per 1k input tokens and $0.0040 per 1k output tokens on Hosted — combined say $0.0065 per 1k tokens. for your short-query workload with batching and caching we might get effective token reduction to 0.6x actual generated tokens which brings down spend. with Dedicated, with a 4xA100 pool and your utilization profile, the effective per-token compute cost could drop to something like $0.002–$0.003 per 1k when amortized against reserved capacity, plus reserved fee. these are illustrative — exact depends on seq lengths, peak concurrency, and utilization.
[03:02] Tom: That delta is significant if we can keep utilization high. Our worry is bursty load — if we reserve capacity we might waste on low days or need burst capacity that adds cost. how does Redwood handle burst?
[03:14] Leo: We have burst pools and autoscale policies; Dedicated customers can configure burst credits or overlay hosted-backed burst for short windows. that keeps a predictable core but lets you handle spikes. billing differs: burst usage above commit is billed at a higher rate.
[03:26] Aisha: For caching — what's involved? are we responsible for building the cache layer or does Redwood provide prefix/KV caching?
[03:33] Leo: Redwood provides transparent prefix/KV caching at the serving runtime for common patterns; you can also integrate with your own cache. we expose hit rates and token-level savings in Console so you can see unit economics.
[03:44] Priya: Security — we need KMS integration, SOC2, and logs for audits. would Private be required?
[03:50] Maya: Not necessarily. Hosted supports customer-managed KMS for key material in some tiers and we have SOC2 attestation. Private gives you a private control plane and optionally on-prem if needed for strict compliance. we can share our security pack after this call.
[04:05] Tom: latency — you're saying 150ms 95th is doable on Hosted?
[04:09] Leo: It depends on model and region. For small models and short sequences, yes — but some models and long-tail sequences will push latency. Dedicated lets you pin lower tail latency because capacity is reserved and we can fine-tune kernel selection. also batching policies add latency; we can set micro-batching to balance tail latency.
[04:27] Aisha: I'd like an example where we compare end-to-end cost and latency for three scenarios: Hosted with autoscale, Dedicated (reserve 4xA100) with burst backfill, and Private VPC deployment.
[04:37] Maya: We'll do that — Leo will run benchmarks with your sample traces.
[04:40] Maya: quick question on budget — Priya, do you have a target spend range for a Q2 pilot?
[04:45] Priya: We're aiming <$60k/month for the pilot phase, ideally closer to $40k. that's for production-like throughput.
[04:52] Maya: good to know. We'll craft options around that.
[04:55] Tom: On instrumentation — what metrics do we get to evaluate cost per request?
[04:59] Leo: Console exposes token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency, batch depth distribution, cache hit rate, and per-token GPU time. you can also drop traces to our tracing hooks.
[05:12] Aisha: How do you attribute costs when batching combines multiple requests? I.e., if 10 small requests are batched, how is cost allocated per request?
[05:19] Leo: We allocate cost based on token share per request within the batch; Console will show per-request attribution and an aggregated per-route cost. it's not perfect but it's standard practice.
[05:30] Speaker 1: (mumbled) and we also allow sample-based attribution when exact tokens are unknown.
[05:36] Maya: on model choices — are you planning to use open models or proprietary models?
[05:40] Aisha: Mostly open models for now; we have some in-house fine-tuning. we care about inference latency and cost.
[05:46] Leo: open models usually compress well with quantization; we can recommend specific model variants that trade-off quality vs cost.
[05:52] Priya: For data residency, we need logs kept in EU. is that supported?
[05:57] Maya: Yes, we have region-specific deployments and Private VPC options for stricter residency. Hosted can also keep logs in region for enterprise accounts.
[06:06] Tom: Any questions about sample trace we'll send? format?
[06:09] Leo: JSONL with timestamp, prompt length, response length, and any metadata is perfect; we mainly need seq length distribution and concurrency timeline.
[06:17] Aisha: We'll give a 7-day sample and highlight a few peak windows.
[06:20] Maya: Perfect.
[06:22] (short pause while someone types)
[06:35] Aisha: One practical item — we currently cache at application layer for user history, would Redwood caching duplicate or complement that?
[06:42] Leo: It complements. Redwood's KV cache is at the inference runtime and can reduce generation tokens for repeated prefixes even if you also have app-level deduping. There's synergy.
[06:52] Tom: About pricing tiers and discounts — do you have a breakpoint for committed usage? e.g., above X tokens we get lower Hosted rates?
[06:58] Maya: Yes we have volume tiers and dedicated pricing for committed contracts. We'll include a tiered pricing sheet in the follow-up with examples for your monthly volumes.
[07:08] Priya: On Dedicated — how long are commitments typically? 6/12/24 months?
[07:11] Maya: Usually 12-months for most customers but we do 6-month pilots and can structure quarterly for proofs with higher per-unit rates.
[07:20] Aisha: We want to run a 6-week pilot with realistic traffic. how do we measure success and what SLA do we expect?
[07:27] Leo: For pilot, define success metrics: 95th latency <150ms, cost < target, and quality delta <2% vs baseline. We'll instrument and run canary traffic.
[07:36] Speaker 2: (inaudible) also recommend including a burst scenario to validate autoscaling.
[07:42] Maya: yep. we'll capture that.
[07:45] Tom: On encryption in transit and at rest — standard TLS and KMS? any HSM options?
[07:51] Maya: TLS in transit and AES-256 at rest; for Private we integrate with customer KMS and HSM-backed keys if required.
[07:59] Aisha: Do you provide cost simulations in advance so we can plug numbers into our finance model?
[08:03] Leo: Yes, we provide a cost model spreadsheet where you drop in seq lengths, cache hit rate, batch depth, and it produces expected spend under Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.
[08:14] Priya: Great, we'll need that for procurement.
[08:18] Maya: We'll send the spreadsheet and an example calculation tied to your volumes.
[08:23] (slight crosstalk)
[08:35] Aisha: One worry — vendor lock-in if we use Redwood-specific caching or private deployment. how portable are configs?
[08:42] Leo: Our APIs are standard REST and SDKs; caching semantics are documented. For Private, you control model artifacts and KMS; switching would require migration but it's similar to common infra migrations.
[08:55] Maya: We often help with migration planning as part of Dedicated/Private engagements.
[09:02] Tom: ok. can you do a quick sanity calc now — assume 50M tokens/month, average effective tokens after caching = 30M, what's rough Hosted cost at your earlier per-1k estimate?
[09:11] Maya: using the earlier $0.0065 per 1k tokens, 30M tokens is 30,000 * $0.0065 = $195, roughly $195k? wait math slip — gotta be careful: 30M tokens / 1k = 30,000 units * $0.0065 = $195. oh that can't be right.
[09:29] Leo: (laughs) small decimal mishap — it's $195 for 30M tokens at $0.0065 per 1k? actually recalc: 30,000 * 0.0065 = 195. But that's $195 not $195k. so per-month $195 seems too low — our units earlier were maybe per 1k inputs + outputs combined — check units.
[09:45] Maya: You're right I'm mixing units. Example earlier was $0.0065 per 1k tokens which is $0.0000065 per token. For 30M tokens that's 30,000 * 0.0065 = $195. So it's actually quite low because per-1k numbers are small. But your budget of $40k-$60k seems to imply different scale or other overheads. Are you counting inference only or also embeddings, storage, etc?
[10:05] Priya: The $40k is for full prod stack including observability, storage, pipeline costs. inference portion we thought would be ~25-40% of that.
[10:13] Leo: ok makes sense. We'll make sure the breakdown aligns.
[10:17] Aisha: For the pilot, we want to try both Hosted and a small Dedicated baseline to compare real costs. can Redwood run both in parallel?
[10:24] Maya: Yes, we can run a hybrid approach and compare. it's a common strategy.
[10:29] Tom: Any pitfalls you often see?
[10:32] Leo: Underestimating cache hit variability and not simulating burst traffic are two big ones. Also mixing quantized models without quality checks can cause regressions.
[10:41] Aisha: Good to know.
[10:44] (brief pause)
[11:00] Maya: ok to recap next steps: we'll send pricing sheet and cost model, Leo will run benchmarks once you send sample traces, security pack and region/residency doc to be shared, and we'll schedule a follow-up deep-dive for Private deployment. Anything to add?
[11:16] Priya: Please include the sample pricing calc for the 4xA100 reserve and the burst scenario.
[11:21] Maya: noted.
[11:23] Tom: I'll send the sample logs by Friday.
[11:27] Aisha: We'll review and get back on budget confirmation.
[11:30] Maya: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with a calendar invite for the deep-dive.
[11:35] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: some speaker labels and short inaudible segments were auto-labeled. There are a few arithmetic slips in the call that were clarified. References to token pricing are illustrative and follow-up deliverables will include exact numbers.
